title: How the Pony Express Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Pony Express, the short-lived 1860-1861 horseback mail service run by the Central Overland California and Pike's Peak Express Company (Russell, Majors and Waddell) between St. Joseph, Missouri and Sacramento. They cover how the relay system of riders, horses, way stations and the mochila mail bag worked, its financial failure, the Pyramid Lake War's impact, legendary riders like Pony Bob Haslam and Billy Fisher, contemporary accounts by Richard Burton and Mark Twain, Buffalo Bill Cody's role in mythologizing it, Mabel Loving's book, and the end of the service when the transcontinental telegraph was completed. The episode ends with a long listener mail segment.
topics: Central Overland California and Pike's Peak Express Company
St. Joseph Missouri to Sacramento mail route

entities.name: Central Overland California and Pike's Peak Express Company

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with off-topic chat about movies, including spoilers for Jaws, before Josh introduces the Pony Express as a famous business failure.

segments.title: Pony Express as a failed business and its purpose
segments.summary: The hosts frame the Pony Express as a business failure that is remembered mainly for its legend. They explain it was a mail service bridging the gap between the eastern telegraph end at St. Joseph, Missouri and Sacramento, California, to speed mail that otherwise took weeks or months.
topics: St. Joseph Missouri to Sacramento mail route

segments.title: How the relay system worked
segments.summary: About eighty young riders, a few horses, and several dozen way stations made up the relay. Horses ran ten to fifteen miles and riders about seventy-five miles, switching horses at stations with the mochila mail bag, which could hold about twenty pounds of mail.

segments.title: Pricing, customers and financial problems
segments.summary: The company charged five dollars per half ounce. The hosts note that the bags rarely held much mail, that customers were mostly newspapers, government and military, and that no official government contract was granted. The business was financially weak.

segments.title: Pyramid Lake War and dangers on the trail
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Pyramid Lake War (Paiute War) of the early 1860s, which raised tensions and attacked way stations, making the job more dangerous. The company lost men and about seventy-five thousand dollars and then increased delivery frequency and lowered prices without success. The hosts note that many popular images of attacks are exaggerated.

segments.title: Legendary riders and contemporary accounts
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Pony Bob Haslam's 380-mile ride, Billy Fisher's snowstorm rescue by a jackrabbit, and contemporary accounts by Richard Burton, who disliked the West, and Mark Twain, who described the riders in Roughing It.

segments.title: Buffalo Bill, myth-making and Pony Express legend
segments.summary: Buffalo Bill Cody's Wild West show featured Pony Express riders and he claimed to have ridden for the company, though he only worked for Alexander Majors as a horseback messenger. Bronco Charlie Miller claimed to be a rider. Movies and fake newspaper ads added to the myth. Buffalo Bill later helped Majors publish his memoir, and Mabel Loving later collected firsthand accounts in a book.

segments.title: Shutdown, aftermath and final facts
segments.summary: The service ended within days of the transcontinental telegraph being completed, in October 1861. The company's founders went broke, and the hosts list delivery statistics, including a record delivery of Lincoln's inaugural address in seven days and seventeen hours and roughly thirty-five thousand pieces of mail.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode with a pointer to the Pony Express trail and a brief note about listener mail to come.
